senses.definition: (mythology) Any member of a race of beings from (especially Scandinavian and other Germanic) folklore, usually depicted as having some sort of supernatural powers and being skilled in crafting and metalworking, often as short with long beards, and sometimes as clashing with elves.

quotes.text: [T]he elf king and his queen made a royal progress every noon with a splendid retinue of dwarves and sprites, […]

quotes.text: Nidavellir, which is sometimes called Svartalfheim, where the dwarfs (who are also known as dark elves) live beneath the mountains and build their remarkable creations.
quotes.reference: 2017, Neil Gaiman, Norse Mythology, Bloomsbury Publishing, page 20:

senses.definition: (now sometimes offensive) A person of short stature, often one whose limbs are disproportionately small in relation to the body as compared with typical adults, usually as the result of a genetic condition.
An animal, plant or other thing much smaller than the usual of its sort.

quotes.text: But none of those brown dwarfs were speeding along on a trajectory that would carry them out of the galaxy like “runaway” hypervelocity stars observed by astronomers in the last two decades.
quotes.reference: 2024 August 21, Ashley Strickland, “An unusual object is moving so fast it could escape the Milky Way. Scientists aren’t certain what it is”, in CNN:

examples: The specimen is a very dwarf form of the plant.
It is possible to grow the plants as dwarf as one desires.

senses.definition: (transitive) To render (much) smaller, turn into a dwarf (version).
(transitive) To make appear (much) smaller, puny, tiny; to be much larger than.
examples: The newly-built skyscraper dwarfs all older buildings in the downtown skyline.

quotes.text: The train bursts from Rusher Cutting Tunnel with explosive violence, the engine's exhaust soaring high into the air, but dwarfed by the mighty limestone cliffs on either side.
quotes.reference: 1960 April, J. P. Wilson, E. N. C. Haywood, “The route through the Peak - Derby to Manchester: Part Two”, in Trains Illustrated, page 225:

quotes.text: In the past two years, NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope has located nearly 3,000 exoplanet candidates ranging from sub-Earth-sized minions to gas giants that dwarf our own Jupiter.
quotes.reference: 2013 May-June, Kevin Heng, “Why Does Nature Form Exoplanets Easily?”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 184:

senses.definition: To hinder from growing to the natural size; to make or keep small; to stunt.

quotes.text: At present the whole sex is in a manner dwarfed and shrunk - into a race of beauties that seems almost another species
quotes.reference: 1710 July 2 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison], “WEDNESDAY, June 22, 1710”, in The Spectator, number 98; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume II, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:

quotes.text: Even the most common moral ideas and affections […] would be stunted and dwarfed, if cut off from a spiritual background.
